entry.title: Grounded - A poem (about time as a fixed anchor)
entry.summary: As I mentioned when writing about my short film, the concept of time has always held a deep pull for me. I often find myself subconsciously capturing it through my photos and also that short film. Revisiting some older poems recently, I noticed the exact…
entry.content:
As I mentioned when writing about my short film, the concept of time has always held a deep pull for me. I often find myself subconsciously capturing it through my photos and also that short film. Revisiting some older poems recently, I noticed the exact same theme at play, especially in Grounded (below). But here, time appears as something permanent: a frozen moment anchored within the flow of lived experience. I’ll be sharing more of these in the coming weeks. I wrote these back in 2023. 

Grounded 

As the clouds passed, there you sat, firm and brave on the land that belonged to you.

Like the skies, and the heights, from which you had seen it all.

And all looked up to you from the ground that held no secrets.

The ground where you ate, and you fed those who came for you.

The water from which you sprung, meandering through the soil, lifting you up on an open hand where a ladybird rests.

Where good fortune and mishap are all, and all things are as judged by the eye of the beholder.

Lifelike. Joyful. Battered. Bandaged and saved.

For your story to be told and sprayed on fences and walls— oh, how they divide us all!

When we fly off in search of an illusion, a meal, a dream, or a place for the night.

Darkness, illuminated by your ever-shining light.

entry.title: Upcoming short film: "Non ci pensare mai" (No time without love, no love without time).
entry.summary: I'm currently working on a short film called "Non ci pensare mai" (No time without love, no love without time). It's a film about love, grief, and the passage of time. For some reason that I cannot quite articulate, the concept of time is something…
entry.content:
I'm currently working on a short film called "Non ci pensare mai" (No time without love, no love without time). It's a film about love, grief, and the passage of time. For some reason that I cannot quite articulate, the concept of time is something that deeply interests me. In photography, this expresses itself as a desire to capture a moment that will never be exactly the same again, the way you experienced it. The very second you realize you are seeing something, it has already changed. Coincidentally (or maybe not, according to Carl Jung), last week I came across this quote by the Dutch poet and writer Cees Buddingh:
"Look around you, look around you. As the world is right now, you will never see it again."
— Cees Buddingh' (1918–1985)
 
This beautifully encapsulates my 'philosophy' when it comes to photography. I guess making a short film about time is just a natural extension of that, though I don't really know for sure. Anyway, for the setting of this film, I chose a remote mountain village in Abruzzo in the year 1970, which I think creates the perfect mood for a story like this. I hope to release it soon!

entry.title: Sun, Shadows and Stone: An afternoon at Valle dei Templi
entry.summary: As we drive into the parking lot of the Valle dei Templi, there's sand and dust everywhere. It's early August and Ferragosto hasn't started yet, but it feels like the whole of Italy has planned to come here today. Cars crisscross the terrain like ants,…
entry.content:
As we drive into the parking lot of the Valle dei Templi, there's sand and dust everywhere. It's early August and Ferragosto hasn't started yet, but it feels like the whole of Italy has planned to come here today. Cars crisscross the terrain like ants, and, in typical Sicilian fashion, there's little signage to tell you where to go. After all these years of traveling to Sicily, I've grown used to a bit of organized chaos. I like it, actually. It makes the island feel so much like itself: a stark contrast to the planned, orderly street architecture I'm used to in the Netherlands.

Today I won't have many opportunities to take photos. Still, when the moment arises, I attempt a few shots. I don't want to disturb our guide as he talks (which he does so well), walking us through the complete history of the valley in just over two hours. For the pictures I do manage to shoot, I've set my camera to RAW. It helps preserve the highlights under this burning sun. What I sometimes like to do in these situations is shoot deliberately into the sun. It gives you a silhouetted foreground, and paired with a vintage 50mm Takumar lens, it creates a really beautiful, warm vintage look.

We conclude the day entirely satisfied. This was such a rich experience. It's incredible to witness how these ancient structures have survived destruction, wars, and natural disasters over the millennia, yet they are still standing: a testament to the people who built them. They knew a thing or two about construction, and so much more besides: agriculture, astronomy, mathematics, things that we, 2000 years later, can still learn from. This visit definitely deserves a follow-up in the form of a good book about these temples. Or who knows, perhaps I'll visit them again someday. They're not in a hurry, after all.

For now, it's back to the dusty parking lot to queue up with my ant friends. I forget about the ancient Greeks for a moment as my mind slowly drifts to granitas and an ice-cold Peroni.
